sections.title: What you know, and what is new
sections.content: You know reported speech with a verb that introduces it: *Pensó que no tenía tiempo*, *Se preguntó dónde estaba Pedro*. In stories there is a third way. The narrator gives a character's thoughts, doubts or feelings **without** a verb like *pensó* and without *que*. This is called free indirect speech. This lesson teaches you to recognise it, so that you read a character's thought as the character's, not as the narrator's opinion.

sections.title: Three ways to tell the same thought
rows: Ana pensó: «¿Dónde está Pedro? Otra vez llega tarde.»
Ana se preguntó dónde estaba Pedro y pensó que otra vez llegaba tarde.
Ana miró el reloj. ¿Dónde estaba Pedro? Otra vez llegaba tarde.

sections.title: How it works
sections.content: Free indirect speech is like reported speech in two ways: it keeps the third person and the past tenses of the narration (*estaba*, *llegaba*, and the conditional for what is still to come). It is like direct speech in two others: it keeps the character's questions and exclamations, and the character's own point of view. That is why a word like *mañana* can stay next to a past verb: *Luis abrió la carta. ¡Por fin! Mañana mismo se lo diría a todos.*

sections.title: Four clues
sections.content:
• There is no *pensó que*, *dijo que* or *se preguntó*, and no quotation marks.
• The sentence is a question, a doubt or an exclamation inside the narration.
• The time and place words belong to the character: *ahora*, *mañana*, *aquí*, *aquello*.
• The verb is in a past tense, but the thought sounds like the character speaking.

items.spanish: Ana miró el reloj. ¿Dónde estaba Pedro?
items.english: Ana looked at the clock. Where was Pedro?

items.spanish: Luis abrió la carta. ¡Por fin! Mañana mismo se lo diría a todos.
items.english: Luis opened the letter. At last! He would tell everyone tomorrow.

items.spanish: El jefe leyó el informe. ¿Quién lo había escrito? Aquello no tenía sentido.
items.english: The boss read the report. Who had written it? That made no sense.

sections.content: You only need to recognise this form, not to write it. When a narrated sentence suddenly asks a question or exclaims, ask: whose thought is this? If it is a character's, it is free indirect speech.
